TK-01.c01: A **tank vehicle** (tanker) carries liquid or gas in a tank; the liquid moves and sits high, so it handles very differently from a truck carrying boxes.
Also study Sections **2, 5, 6, and 9**: Driving Safely, Air Brakes, Combination Vehicles, and Hazardous Materials.
**Inspect the tanker before loading, unloading, or driving it**, so it is safe to carry the load and safe to drive.
**Surge** is liquid sloshing in a tank that is not full; **outage** is the empty space left at the top so the liquid can expand.
TK-01.c02: You need an **N endorsement** when your vehicle needs a **Class A, B, or C** CDL and you haul a liquid or liquid gas in tanks.
Tank sizes: **more than 119 gallons** per individual tank **and** **1,000 gallons or more** aggregate (total), attached permanently or temporarily.
The liquid **does not have to be HazMat**; milk or water counts too.
[CA] An empty storage tank not designed for transport, **at least 1,000 gallons**, temporarily attached to a flatbed trailer is **not a tank vehicle**.
[CA] A **CLP** holder with N may drive a tank vehicle **only if it is empty** (purged if it held HazMat); new Class C with only N needs a skills test, adding N doesn't.
TK-01.c03: On **all** tank vehicles, the most important thing to check for is **leaks**; look under and around the vehicle.
Hauling liquid or gas in a leaking tank is a **crime**: you are cited, stopped from driving further, and may have to pay for the cleanup.
Intake, discharge, and cut-off **valves** must be in the correct position before loading, unloading, or moving.
Check the shell for dents or leaks, pipes and hoses especially **around joints**, manhole covers for **gaskets** that close correctly, and keep vents clear.
Tankers come in many types, so check the **operator's manual** to learn how to inspect yours.
TK-01.c04: If your tanker has them, make sure these **work**: vapor recovery kits, grounding and bonding cables, emergency shutoff systems, and a built-in fire extinguisher.
**Never** drive a tank vehicle with **open valves** or **open manhole covers**.
Find out what **emergency equipment** your vehicle is required to carry, and make sure you have it and it works.
TK-01.c05: Tankers need special care for **2 reasons**: the **high center of gravity** and the movement of the liquid (**surge**).
Much of the load's weight rides high above the road, so a tanker is **top-heavy** and easy to roll over.
Figure 8.1: a tanker's center of gravity is about **60–78 inches** high; a pickup truck's is about **18–24 inches**.
Tests show tankers can roll over **at the posted curve speed**, so take highway curves and ramps **well below** it.
TK-01.c06: **Surge** is liquid moving in a **partially filled** tank, and it hurts handling.
When you stop, the wave hits the end of the tank and **pushes the truck** in the direction the wave is moving.
On a slippery road like ice, surge can **shove a stopped truck** out into an intersection.
TK-01.c07: **Bulkheads** are solid walls dividing a tank into smaller tanks; when loading and unloading, watch **weight distribution** so the front or rear is not too heavy.
**Baffles** are bulkheads **with holes**; they control forward-and-back surge, but **side-to-side** surge can still happen and cause a rollover.
A **smooth bore** (unbaffled) tank has nothing to slow the liquid, so forward-and-back surge is very strong; be extremely careful **starting and stopping**.
Food tankers such as **milk** tankers are usually smooth bore because **sanitation rules forbid baffles**, which make the tank hard to clean.
TK-01.c08: **Never load a cargo tank totally full**; liquids expand as they warm, and the room you leave is called **outage**.
Different liquids expand by different amounts, so you must **know the outage requirement** for your load.
A full tank of a **dense liquid**, like some acids, may be **over the legal weight limit**, so heavy liquids are often loaded only part way.
How much to load depends on **4 things**: expansion, weight of the liquid, legal weight limits, and temperature; for "3 things", answer expansion, weight, and legal limits.
TK-01.c09: [CA] Speeding with **more than 500 gallons** of flammable liquid, or driving with willful or wanton disregard for safety, brings a **fine** on the first offense.
[CA] A 2nd or later offense within **2 years** → a fine plus suspension of up to **6 months** of your HazMat and/or N endorsement.
[CA] A tank vehicle with a capacity over **500 gallons** hauling flammable liquid: you may drive **at most 10 hours** in a work period.
TK-01.c10: **Start, slow down, and stop very smoothly**, and make smooth turns and lane changes.
To control surge, keep **steady brake pressure** and don't release too soon; brake far ahead of the stop and increase following distance.
In a quick stop, use **controlled or stab braking**; steering quickly while braking can roll the tanker over.
Curves: **slow down before**, then accelerate slightly through; the posted curve speed may be too fast for a tanker.
Wet roads **double** stopping distance, and **empty tankers may take longer** to stop than full ones; a skidding tank trailer may jackknife.
